books.title: Shape of Time
books.subtitle: Oakland, and elsewhere
books.description: Jay meets Tan across an ordinary counter in Oakland. Before he agrees to travel with her, he needs to know what the invitation will cost and what will still belong to him.

blocks.text: The woman at the counter wanted clef, one bottle, and Jay pulled it slim and cold from the case behind him and set it by the register. Eleven forty on a Tuesday, two people in line behind her, and everything about the sale was ordinary until he turned the shop phone toward her with the payment screen up. She held her palm flat above the glass and waited. The phone did nothing. She waited longer, moved her hand in a small circle, then looked at him. "Did you change something on this?" "It's the same phone," Jay said. "You tap it." She tapped the edge of the screen as if it might open. Behind her, the man with the six-pack shifted his weight.

Her face went careful, which is what embarrassment looks like on someone out of practice at it. Jay had watched enough visitors stall at this counter to know the look. He turned the phone face down before the line could get interested, bagged the bottle, and slid it across. "On me. Come back when you've figured the phone out." She didn't move. The broken payment she understood; the machine had failed her, and machines fail. A bag on the counter with no charge against it fit nothing she knew. She picked it up as if the price might be hidden somewhere inside, thanked him in a tone that made it a question, and gave up her place in line.

plate.alt: In a worn Oakland shop, Tan stands at the counter opposite Jay while two customers wait; a bag and face-down phone sit between them.
plate.narrativeJob: Fix Jay and Tan as the two people this book will keep returning to, and establish the shop as a local business partly refitted for visitor money, with attention distributed unequally around Tan's failure at the counter.
plate.proseWithholds: What the shop actually is: how a visitor-facing refit sits on top of years of working wear, how the queue arranges itself in the narrow space, and who is looking at whom in the moment after the failed payment. The prose does not describe the room or the distribution of attention; the plate supplies both.

blocks.text: She came back Thursday night with paper money folded in her jacket pocket, counted before she reached the counter. "I thought you were working an angle," she said. "Free bottle, then some hook later. I owed you an apology for thinking it, so here it is." She laid down enough for two bottles of clef. Jay pulled one cold from the case and took payment for that bottle only, sliding the rest of the bills back across the glass. "The first one was a gift. You don't get to buy it back." She looked at the money as if the rule were written on it somewhere, then pocketed it. "Tan," she said. "Jay." Nobody was in line, so they kept talking.

She stayed by the ice cream case while he rang up cigarettes and scratchers, asking questions between customers, none of them stupid. At eleven he cut the lights and pulled the gate down, and she walked with him toward the bus stop at the corner. "My guide says this stop is original," she said. "Standing longer than your shop." Jay pointed half a block up, where four epoxy-filled circles sat in the sidewalk in a tidy rectangle. "Shelter posts. The stop was there until spring, when the city striped a coach bay for the tour buses. Everything waiting for the 72 got moved down here." She studied the capped bolts for a while and did not ask him what else in the neighborhood was wrong. "When do you work next?" she asked.

The band was a four-piece in the back room of a bar on Telegraph: trumpet, upright bass, drums, and a guitarist who sang with his eyes shut. Neither of them called these meetings accidents anymore. Jay had told Tan when the show was, and she had come. They stood in the middle of the crowd, her shoulder against his chest, his hand at her waist because there was nowhere else to put it, and neither of them moved. Midway through the third song she hummed a line, low, and four beats later the trumpet played it. Jay bent to her ear. "You know this one." "Track nine," she said. "There's a compilation where I'm from. Oakland, this decade. I've had it since I was sixteen. The credit says performer unknown."

Jay watched the trumpet player, a heavy man in a church shirt with sweat standing on his forehead. "Does he get anything? When it sells where you're from." Tan kept her eyes on the stage. "I don't know," she said. "I paid for that album twice, once when I lost the first copy. I never asked where the money went." She did not dress it up with a guess about licensing, and he liked her better for it. The song ended, the room shouted, the guitarist counted the next one in fast, and Tan pulled Jay's arm around her and leaned back into him.

plate.alt: Jay stands behind Tan in a crowded bar as a four-piece band plays; at the room’s edge, a man raises a small recorder.
plate.narrativeJob: Show that the music Jay and Tan are enjoying is being taken down tonight, connecting the uncredited compilation Tan owns to a plausible source in this very room, while the couple remains inside the pleasure of the performance and does not see it happening.
plate.proseWithholds: That the performance is being recorded tonight by a visitor at the edge of the room, unnoticed by Jay and Tan. The prose establishes that a recording of this music exists and sells at Tan's home coordinate; only the image shows a recording being made.

blocks.text: Outside the bar the sidewalk was emptying, and Tan kept hold of Jay's arm instead of letting the crowd sort them apart. "I planned this trip around your shifts," she said. "I asked which nights you worked and booked my crossing so I'd land on a Tuesday." Jay admitted he had told her about the show before he knew whether the band was still together, in case she was already checking his schedule. She laughed once, and he kissed her, or she kissed him; afterward neither would concede the point. Then she stepped back half a pace and held both his hands. "I go home tomorrow. My crossing window is booked. I'll come back Thursday."

"Which Thursday," Jay said. "Name it. There are a lot of Thursdays standing out here, and you could walk into any of them." She thought about it seriously instead of laughing it off, and he watched her count. "The seventeenth. Your seventeenth." "And what does that cost you? How long do you live between now and then?" "Twenty hours out, if the currents behave. Four or five days at home. A day and a half back, because the return leg fights you the whole way." She ticked the legs off on his fingers, not her own. "Call it a week for me. Twelve days for you." "Thursday the seventeenth," Jay said. "I'll put a bottle at the back of the case where nobody reaches, and you'll be a week older when you drink it." "Deal," she said, and both of them meant the same night.

She came back on the seventeenth, an hour before close, with the week showing on her. "The return leg fought me," she said. Jay brought out the bottle he had kept twelve days at the back of the case, and she drank it at the counter while he counted the register. After he pulled the gate she took his arm. "There's a place by the lake I want to show you. Travelers go there. I want you to see us when we're not visiting."

The place was a second floor above a shuttered bank, a lit stairway and a man at a podium with a list. He found Tan's name and looked at Jay. "Guides wait downstairs. There's coffee." "He's with me," Tan said. The man made a mark and stepped aside. On the stairs she squeezed Jay's hand, pleased with how she had handled it.

They lasted an hour. On the sidewalk she asked what was wrong, and he told her. "You didn't say he was wrong about me. You said you were allowed to bring me. With me covers a guide. It covers a porter, or a date somebody's paying for. He picks which, and you decide whether I get up the stairs at all." She began to say she had only meant to get him in, and stopped, because that was what he had just described. At the corner she said good night. She didn't name a Thursday, and he didn't ask for one.

Tan came in ten minutes before close, bought nothing, and stood clear of the register until the last customer left. "You were right about the stairs," she said. "I'm not asking you to pretend it didn't happen. I want to do better." Jay started to answer and saw the water instead, a slow sheet coming from under the cold case. The drain line had plugged again. He went for the mop. Tan hung her jacket on the door handle and asked where he kept the towels.

They emptied the bottom shelf together, moved the clef and beer to the other case, and argued about the fix. She wanted to shut the unit down and let it thaw overnight; he said the stock wouldn't last and the landlord didn't answer calls. She found the drain pan, straightened wire off a hanger, and cleared the line, and when the trapped water let go over her wrists she laughed hard enough that he laughed too. They mopped side by side and restocked the shelf her way, which was better.

He walked her out under the half-lowered gate. "Come see where I live," she said. "Not a visit list. My place. My father can get an application considered. That part is real." "Who sponsors me," Jay said. "What does the crossing take out of me. If we come apart there, how do I get home." She took each question seriously and could not answer any of them. "Then find out," he said. "When you have facts, I'll listen."

Tan came in on a Monday with an aluminum case and set it on the break table in the back room, between the microwave and the register tape. Inside were three printed sheets under a clear film, and when she squared the film to its corner marks a route appeared across all three. "Primas is the one you'd guess," she said. "Phantas and Mystas are the other two. Your crossing runs mostly Primas Major, with one Phantas correction here, at a station." Jay put his thumb near the line. "What does it feel like?" "Motion. About twenty hours of it for your body. You're older at the far end, whichever direction you ride."

He asked who could change the route. She touched the printed lanes with the company's mark, then the penciled numbers crowding the margins. "The printed part is licensed. The company redraws it, and you travel on the new sheet or not at all. The pencil is what independent mappers observed last month and traded. Nobody owns that." Each sheet bore a revision stamp; this set was six weeks stale. The gray shading around the Phantas correction meant low confidence, and it had been gray when the ink was new. The maps were always becoming wrong. "If a current shifts under you, you stop at the nearest station and wait to be re-plotted. You do not push through." She never rounded a number, and he watched her hands as much as the chart. "Leave it with me tonight," he said. "I want to read it slow."

plate.alt: Tan points across a sprawling annotated paper route map on the shop’s back-room table while Jay studies it beside her.
plate.narrativeJob: Shows the reader what Jay is actually being asked to trust: a physical navigational chart whose printed corporate lanes, hand-traded margin observations, revision stamps, and gray low-confidence zones make the difficulty of temporal travel and the unequal ownership of its knowledge legible at a glance, while keeping the moment a quiet working scene between two people at a break table.
plate.proseWithholds: How the route physically reads: the relative extent of the printed, company-stamped lanes versus the handwritten traded observations in the margins; how much of the chart sits under gray low-confidence shading, especially around the Phantas correction; and how visibly dated and provisional the revision stamps make the sheets appear.

apertures.quote: The maps were always becoming wrong

blocks.text: The answers came on paper, one envelope at a time, the way Jay had asked. A sponsorship letter naming the company, with a case number. A note over her father's signature saying the application would be heard this quarter. Last, from a return carrier, a passage issued in Jay's own name, documents he would hold himself. He still could not read a live map or run a PRMTT; a crew would carry him both ways. But the papers drew a line around what he could not do. He copied everything at the print shop on San Pablo, put one set in the shop safe and one behind his refrigerator, and asked the owner for three weeks off. The dates went up on the calendar behind the register.

Tan came in on a Tuesday, and he told her with the register open. "Conditions first. The return passage stays mine. If a current shifts, we stop at a station and wait, your rule, and I'll hold you to it. Wherever we go in your time, I get in under my own name, or we don't go in." She agreed to each one without dressing any of them up. "Now the rest," Jay said. "I love you. I want to see the place that made you. Your kitchen, your street, whatever your version of the 72 stop is. I want us to exist on your ground too, not only on mine." The door chimed behind her. "So yes," he said, and turned to the next customer.

movementRest.continuation: The next movement begins with the application and the physical crossing. Shape of Time continues.

books.title: The Map on the Wall
books.subtitle: Lagos lagoon route notes
books.description: On the last scheduled municipal ferry run, Eniola disputes a licensed route, records the crossing, and makes the evidence public.

origin.quote: The maps were always becoming wrong

blocks.text: Forty minutes into the last scheduled run, the company console ordered a return. Eniola Akinyemi checked it twice. The licensed chart still showed the Phantas Minor current where it had run in April, but her field vanes read it half a point closer to the crossing line, and three paper soundings witnessed this week agreed with the vanes. The return leg would carry the ferry broadside through the shifted current. Her credential was probationary and the console logged every override. Behind her sat eleven passengers with work shifts, a school pickup, a mother waiting at the inhabited coordinate.

She walked the deck with the sounding book open. "State what you observe. I'm recording your name." Pilot Ropo Balogun gave his circle rate and the drag he'd felt on the second circuit. Chidi, the mirror technician, gave the flux angle off the array. Mrs. Adeyemi, who had ridden this crossing for thirty years, recited Tuesday's soundings from memory, and they matched the paper. Eniola wrote each name, then disabled the automatic return and read out the corrected line.

The crossing took two hours of work. Balogun held the ferry in tightened circles until his shoulders shook. Chidi reset the mirrors by hand every few minutes because the corrected line ran oblique to the licensed one, and the heat exchanger had to be trimmed each time. Eniola called small corrections until her voice went dry. When the outer berth's lamp finally resolved, the passengers stood up stiffly and gathered their bags, and she signed the sounding book beneath their names.

The console locked while Mrs. Adeyemi was still on the gangway. SUSPENDED PENDING REVIEW, her credential number, and nothing else she could open. An officer named Wale came down the berth with a receipt for the sounding book and the wheelhouse key, and Eniola handed both over, but not before she had copied the run onto the back of a printed timetable: the return order at 18:41, each correction with its witness, the time of every vane reading. Then she chalked the whole trace on the terminal wall beside the fare notice, the licensed line and the corrected one and the point where the current had actually crossed.

Crews came off the late runs and read it. The Makoko pilot added her own trace in a different hand, and it sat a quarter point off Eniola's at the crossing. A navigator from the Epe circuit added a third that agreed with neither. Wale returned with an order to clear the wall and read it aloud while Balogun copied the chalk into his book and Chidi photographed it on a passenger's phone. Eniola cleaned the wall herself, since the order named her, and it changed nothing she cared about. The lines were in a dozen books now, three versions of one current, and the outer stops would run tomorrow on whichever version their navigators believed.

plate.alt: At a Lagos ferry terminal at night, Eniola chalks conflicting route traces while crews copy them, an officer reads an order, and a ferry waits behind.
plate.narrativeJob: The map has moved from a licensed console and a single sounding book onto a public wall carrying at least three materially incompatible traces in different hands.
plate.proseWithholds: The scale of dissemination and dependence that the prose does not enumerate: how many crews are actually recording the wall into their own books, and the departure board tying the disputed crossing to the named outer stops whose morning runs will follow one trace or another.

movementRest.label: The last ferry
movementRest.continuation: The next movement asks how a public correction earns trust after Eniola's credential is gone. The Map on the Wall continues.
